title: Engineered Maternal Cells and Selective Dosage Compensation in Trisomy 21: A Research Framework Centered on Maternal Production and a Candidate Protein–RNA System
content: The central question of this article is whether maternal cells can be engineered into a production and delivery platform that supplies functional molecular tools to cells from offspring with trisomy 21. Studies of maternal microchimerism and tolerance to non-inherited maternal antigens (NIMAs) provide a basis for examining the biological significance of mother–offspring matching. Delivery by engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) and XIST-mediated silencing of chromosome 21 provide experimental precedents for molecular transport and chromosome dosage regulation, respectively. On this basis, we propose that, with the maternal producer cells, recipient model, and candidate cargo clearly defined, products generated by maternal cells engineered ex vivo could enable controllable local molecular regulation or broader chromosome dosage compensation in a patient's own cells. If these engineered products retain relevant maternal antigenic features, mother–offspring matching might also improve recipient compatibility at an equivalent target effect. The principal candidate developed here is the P-type system, provisionally named T21-DoseSwitch-P: maternal cells would produce an NLS-bearing dCas9–KRAB protein, which would form a candidate complex with a separate guide RNA (gRNA), for investigation of EV-mediated delivery, local expression regulation, and cellular function. The regulatory core builds on established CRISPRi architecture; the connection between maternal production and effective delivery is the central untested proposition. XIST expression cargo and installation tools form an independently investigable extension toward chromosome-wide effects, while exogenous RNA tethering remains a separate exploratory branch. A documented example of target-homolog selection, route-specific cargo definitions and size references, analysis of production and delivery conflicts, and comparisons that distinguish source effects from cargo effects are used to formulate predictions that different research teams can test independently. The most discriminating findings would establish whether maternal products produce intracellular effects attributable to their cargo, whether matching provides an independent benefit, and whether the same platform can connect establishment of an XIST expression source to chromosome-wide correction of expression. This article presents a mechanistic hypothesis and reports no original experimental or efficacy data; its purpose is to narrow the range of research questions that merit priority testing.
